Outside the building, Christoph Leamas, Alec's son, a criminal with nothing to lose, follows Guillam and demands money with threats, while Karen Gold, Liz's daughter, wants only to know why her mother died. Guillam, cornered, works out and finally admits what the operations were for. Mundt, the East German operations chief, had been recruited by the Circus, and Tulip was killed by him because she could have exposed him; the Circus concealed her murder to protect its source. Windfall was built to defend that source, and Leamas and Liz Gold were sent into it without being told they were expendable.

Guillam gives the enquiry what he judges it is entitled to, refuses to invent what would suit it, and leaves London before the settlement is concluded, aware that the Service will arrange the record to protect itself whatever he says. He goes to Germany and, after some searching, finds George Smiley in a library in Freiburg: very old, still working, and entirely clear-eyed about what was done. Smiley confirms the whole of it. Mundt was theirs; Tulip died by his hand and the Circus buried it; Leamas and Liz Gold were used and lost in the same cause; and the men who ordered it understood the cost. Asked what it was for, Smiley answers that he served his country while he could believe in it, and that if there was a larger purpose behind the whole cold enterprise it was Europe. He offers Guillam no absolution and takes none for himself. Guillam returns to Brittany with the past finally spoken aloud and nothing about it undone.

aliases: the Wicked Witch of the West
characters.description: The green-skinned woman remembered across Oz as the Wicked Witch of the West, dead for years by the time this book opens. Her book of magic, the Grimmerie, her broom, and anyone descended from her are still being hunted by the government of Loyal Oz, which is the only reason Brrr has employment at all.
characters.name: Elphaba

characters.description: The Witch's presumed son, grown and long since vanished from public view. What became of him, of the Grimmerie, and of any child of his are precisely the questions the Emperor's court has sent an agent out to ask.
characters.name: Liir

characters.description: The Cowardly Lion of legend, now middle-aged, titled, and working for the Emperor's court as a collector of debts and information. He arrives at a rural cloister standing in the path of an advancing army, carrying a commission to interview an ancient woman kept in its crypt, and his own reasons for needing the errand to succeed: his standing, his property and his liberty are all provisional. Vain about his appearance, easily wounded, and thoroughly practised at the retreat that earned him his name.
characters.name: Brrr

characters.description: An impossibly old woman shut away in the crypt beneath the cloister because she will not die. Blind, cracked, and perfectly lucid when it suits her, she agrees to give her interrogator an account of her life in exchange for something of his. Her testimony is the strangest thing in the book: she cannot say where she came from, remembers no childhood at all, and suspects she was made rather than born, for a purpose bound up with the Witch's family.
characters.name: Yackle

characters.description: A veiled, self-contained woman who travels with Brrr and the Clock company and is, by the arrangement between them, his companion. She keeps her face and her history covered, speaks little of either, and has made herself unreachable in a way Brrr has learned not to press.
characters.name: Ilianora

characters.description: The bad-tempered dwarf who owns and drives the Clock of the Time Dragon, a travelling theatrical contraption that stages prophetic tableaux for whatever audience it can find. He claims the Clock is older than Oz and that he is bound to it rather than the other way round, and he takes an interest in the cloister that has nothing to do with anyone's commission.
characters.name: Mr. Boss

characters.description: The elderly head of the Cloister of Saint Glinda, presiding over an evacuation: the war has reached the district and the house stands in the army's line of march. She grants the visiting Lion access to her crypt and its occupant with a briskness suggesting she would be glad to be rid of the problem.
characters.name: The Superior Maunt

characters.description: The ruler of Loyal Oz, who governs as a religious figure and is the dead Witch's younger brother. Brrr does not deal with him face to face, but the commission that sends the Lion to the cloister comes from that court, and what it wants is the Witch's book of magic and any surviving trace of her line.
characters.name: The Emperor Apostle

characters.description: A young human soldier, lost and badly hurt, whom Brrr comes across in the Great Gillikin Forest when the Lion is barely more than a cub. He is the first person to treat the young Lion as company rather than as an animal. He dies of his injuries, and what he leaves behind fixes itself in Brrr's mind for the rest of his life.
characters.name: Jemmsy

characters.description: The clouded, insubstantial dead who linger in the deepest part of the Great Gillikin Forest, hungry for news of the living world. The cub who stumbles into them can tell them nothing worth having, and they let him go with a poor opinion of him. It is the first of many occasions on which Brrr is found wanting and knows it.
characters.name: The Ozmists

characters.description: A short, brisk Munchkinlander maunt who runs the cloister's dispensary and knows a good deal more about what grows in the surrounding hills than her superiors realize. Decades of convent life have made her busy rather than devout.
characters.name: Little Daffy

characters.description: An Ivory Tiger of a proud northern clan, striking, sardonic, and entirely unimpressed by the Lion who attaches himself to her. She has contempt for Animals who make themselves useful to human government and no patience for Brrr's need to be liked. He follows her anyway.
characters.name: Muhlama H'aekeem

characters.description: The girl from another world who turns up in Oz and collects, on her way to the Emerald City, a scarecrow, a tin man and a lion. Brrr joins her party more or less by accident, and the fame and the medal that come out of it define the rest of his public life, mostly to his cost.
characters.name: Dorothy

recaps.ending: Yackle finishes her deposition on her own terms. She reveals that the Grimmerie, the Witch's book of magic, has been hidden beneath the Cloister of Saint Glinda all along, and she gives it up not to the Emperor's court but to Brrr and the company he travels with. Her long refusal to die ends with the handing over: whatever she was made for is discharged, and she is put in the ground, willingly, and stays there. Brrr then makes the first uncowardly choice of his life by defaulting on his commission. He keeps the book, walks away from his title and his creditors at court, and leaves with the dwarf Mr. Boss, the veiled Ilianora, whose history reaches back into the Witch's own household, and Little Daffy, the dispensing maunt, who abandons the convent to go with them. The cloister is left empty for the advancing army. The war between Loyal Oz and Munchkinland is still escalating, the Emperor still wants the Grimmerie and still wants the Witch's descendants, and a green-skinned child of that line is somewhere in the country, unaccounted for. The Clock of the Time Dragon rolls on with the most sought-after object in Oz aboard it and a disgraced Lion walking alongside.
recaps.in_short: The Cowardly Lion, now titled, indebted and working as an agent of the Emperor's court, arrives at a rural cloister in the path of an advancing army with orders to interrogate its strangest inhabitant: Yackle, an ancient woman shut in the crypt because she cannot manage to die. What the court wants from her is the Witch's book of magic and any surviving trace of the Witch's family. The novel alternates their two testimonies. Yackle cannot say where she came from, remembers no childhood, and suspects she was made for a purpose tied to the Witch's line. Brrr recounts his whole life: waking as a cub alone in the forest, the dying soldier Jemmsy, the Ozmists who found him useless, years of failing to belong among either Animals or humans, an errand for the Emerald City that ended in other creatures' deaths and his own escape, and the accidental fame of walking to the Emerald City with Dorothy. In the end Yackle produces the Grimmerie from beneath the cloister, is at last allowed to die, and Brrr, instead of delivering the book to the Emperor, takes it and goes.

recaps.text: Previously in the series: Elphaba Thropp, born green, grew from a dissident student into the sworn enemy of the Wizard who ruled Oz, retreated to the mountain castle of Kiamo Ko, and became the figure Oz remembers as the Wicked Witch of the West. She died there when a girl from another world, Dorothy, threw water on her. Left behind were her book of magic, the Grimmerie, her broom, and Liir, a boy of about fifteen whom she never acknowledged as her son and never disowned. In Son of a Witch, Liir searched the Emerald City and the prison of Southstairs for Nor, the girl carried off from Kiamo Ko by soldiers, served in the Emperor's forces long enough to take part in an atrocity in Quadling Country, and traced a wave of aerial killings to a secret stable of war dragons, which he burned. Shot out of the sky, he was nursed back to health at a rural cloister by a Quadling girl called Candle, who afterwards bore him a green-skinned daughter and hid her from the government. Meanwhile the Wizard's throne passed to the Scarecrow and then to an Emperor Apostle who rules Oz as a living saint and who is Elphaba's own brother, Shell. The country has since split: Munchkinland has seceded, and Loyal Oz is at war with it over water.

Loyal Oz and Munchkinland are at war, and the army's line of march runs through the Cloister of Saint Glinda, a rural convent whose maunts are packing to evacuate. Into this arrives Brrr, the Cowardly Lion of legend, now a titled and thoroughly compromised agent of the Emperor's court, travelling with the Clock of the Time Dragon, its owner the dwarf Mr. Boss, and a veiled woman called Ilianora. His commission is to interview the cloister's oldest and least explicable resident: Yackle, an ancient woman kept in the crypt because she cannot manage to die. The court wants what she knows about the Witch's book of magic and about anyone left of the Witch's family. Yackle agrees to talk, on terms of her own, and begins an account of her life that satisfies nobody. She has no memory of being young, no idea where she came from, and a firm suspicion that she was made rather than born, and made for a purpose she never chose. Brrr, who needs this errand to succeed more than he will admit to anyone, settles in to listen.

Against Yackle's testimony the book sets Brrr's own, beginning at the beginning. He woke as a cub alone in the Great Gillikin Forest with no parents, no pride and no name, and had to work out what he was from scratch. Wandering deeper in, he blundered into the Ozmists, the crowding dead of the forest, who wanted news of the living world and found the cub had none to give. He also found a young human soldier named Jemmsy, lost and dying of his injuries, and stayed with him: the first creature ever to treat him as company. Jemmsy died, and the memory of him, and of what he left behind, became the standard the Lion measured himself against ever afterwards. Brrr came out of the forest having learned that he was conspicuous, unaffiliated and easily shamed. Yackle, meanwhile, describes surfacing into an existence already old, keeping herself by fortune-telling and by being a shopkeeper's oddity, and finding that her path crossed the Thropp family's again and again without her ever being told why.

Brrr's account continues through years of trying and failing to belong. He was taken up briefly by humans as a curiosity, tried and failed to find a place among other Animals, and discovered that Oz under the Wizard was no country for a talking beast without a patron: the Animal population was being pushed out of the professions, off the land, and eventually into hiding. Being neither wild enough to disappear nor connected enough to be protected, he made himself useful to whoever would have him, which is the beginning of everything he is later ashamed of. Yackle's own testimony keeps circling the same problem from the other side. She has watched Oz change across a span no ordinary life covers, has turned up repeatedly at the edges of the Thropp family's story, and cannot say whether she was steering events or was merely put where they were going to happen.

The most damaging stretch of Brrr's history. Employed by the Emerald City's authorities, he was sent north on official business among Animals who had every reason to distrust anyone arriving with a government commission. He was by then entangled with Muhlama H'aekeem, an Ivory Tiger of a proud northern clan who despised exactly the accommodation he had made, and who let him follow her without ever pretending to want him. When the errand went wrong, Brrr saved himself. Others did not get out. Whether that made him a traitor or merely a coward is a question the book puts to the reader rather than answering, but it cost him what standing he had among Animals and left him permanently in debt to the human government that had sent him.

Brrr's public career reached its one moment of glory by pure accident. A girl from another world, Dorothy, was walking to the Emerald City with a scarecrow and a tin man, and the Lion fell in with them. What followed made him famous, and the Wizard's court awarded him a medal for a courage he did not feel he had earned, in front of an audience that would go on remembering it. The fame did not survive the Wizard's departure. Brrr came out of the affair with a title, a reputation he could not live up to, and obligations to whichever government held Oz next, which is how he became a debt collector working the provinces on the court's account. At the cloister, the interview grinds on, Yackle giving up her story in exchange for scraps of his, and neither of them yet saying plainly what they actually want.

The war catches up with the cloister: the army is close, the maunts finish their evacuation, and the interview in the crypt runs out of time. Brrr's later history closes the gap to the present. How he came by his title, how he came to be travelling with the Clock of the Time Dragon and its dwarf, and how he met the veiled Ilianora, whose withheld past turns out to run straight back into the Witch's household at Kiamo Ko. Yackle, for her part, comes to the point. She knows the cloister better than anyone living, she has been part of the Witch's story since before the Witch was born, and she has been waiting a very long time for someone to ask her the right question.

Yackle gives Brrr what the court sent him for and then refuses to let the court have it. Beneath the cloister she leads him, the dwarf and Ilianora to what has been hidden there: the Grimmerie, the Witch's book of magic, put out of reach in the crypt and left in the keeping of a woman nobody believed. Having handed it on, Yackle is at last permitted to stop. She is laid in the ground, and this time the ground keeps her. Brrr does not take the book to the Emperor. He leaves with the Clock company and the Grimmerie instead, giving up his title, his commission and any prospect of being forgiven by the court, and takes on the protection of what is left of the Witch's inheritance. Little Daffy, the cloister's dispensing maunt, walks out of the convent with them. The army moves into the emptied buildings behind them, the war goes on, and the Lion who has run from everything all his life is now carrying the most dangerous object in Oz.

characters.description: A gifted but intensely private young lawyer who has recently moved to New York with three college friends. He walks with difficulty because of an old injury, sometimes suffers disabling episodes of pain, and refuses to explain either his childhood or the source of his scars. He is generous to his friends but reluctant to accept care from them.
characters.name: Jude St. Francis

characters.description: Jude's roommate and closest friend, an aspiring actor who supports himself with restaurant work while seeking roles. Kind, observant, and patient, he is the member of the group most alert to Jude's physical pain and the limits Jude places around his past.
characters.name: Willem Ragnarsson

characters.description: One of the four college friends beginning adult life in New York. JB is ambitious, witty, and socially confident, and plans to build a career as a visual artist. His paintings draw on images of his friends and their shared world.
characters.name: JB Marion

characters.description: The fourth member of the central group, raised in an affluent New York family and training to become an architect. Reserved and uncertain of his place in his own household, he envies the apparent decisiveness of his friends while trying to establish an independent career.
characters.name: Malcolm Irvine

characters.description: Jude's longtime physician and friend. He treats the recurring infections and pain caused by Jude's damaged legs, urges him to protect his health, and recognizes signs that Jude tries to hide from everyone else.
characters.name: Andy Contractor

characters.description: A law professor who becomes Jude's mentor and offers him a form of steady parental affection. Harold is intellectually curious, warm, and persistent without demanding an account of the history Jude will not discuss.
characters.name: Harold Stein

characters.description: Harold's wife, who joins him in welcoming Jude into their home and family. Her calm affection helps make their house a place where Jude can participate in family life without having to explain himself.
characters.name: Julia

characters.description: The social worker who cared for Jude during adolescence and helped him prepare for college. Although she died before the friends' New York years, Jude remembers her as one of the first adults to give him practical help and insist that a different future was possible.
characters.name: Ana

characters.description: A senior partner at the firm where Jude builds his legal career. Demanding but impressed by Jude's ability and discipline, Lucien becomes an important professional mentor.
characters.name: Lucien Voigt

characters.description: An artist in the friends' wider New York circle. Richard owns the building where Jude later lives and offers friendship without pressing Jude for explanations he is unwilling to give.
characters.name: Richard

characters.description: A confident fashion executive whom Jude meets in middle age. Sophisticated, attentive, and direct in his interest, Caleb becomes Jude's first serious romantic partner.
characters.name: Caleb Porter

characters.description: A monk from the monastery where Jude spent his earliest years. He singled Jude out for attention and presented himself as a protector, making him a central figure in Jude's fragmentary memories of childhood.
characters.name: Brother Luke

recaps.ending: After Willem, Malcolm, and Sophie die in a car crash, Jude loses the future that had made his life feel bearable. Harold, Julia, Andy, Richard, and JB remain connected to him, but their care cannot stop his worsening isolation, self-harm, and conviction that the violence of his childhood has permanently defined him. Jude eventually dies by suicide. In the final section Harold looks back on the son he adopted, trying to hold together gratitude for their years as a family with anger and grief over the suffering he could not prevent. JB, the only surviving member of the original group of four, remains part of Harold's life, and their shared memories preserve Jude and their dead friends without resolving the loss.
recaps.in_short: Four college friends begin adult life together in New York: actor Willem, artist JB, architect Malcolm, and lawyer Jude. Their careers flourish and their friendships survive envy, addiction, separation, and reconciliation, but Jude conceals a childhood of exploitation and violence as well as continuing self-harm. Professor Harold Stein and his wife Julia adopt him, while Willem becomes first his most trusted friend and later his partner. Jude experiences a period of stability and love, yet never escapes the belief that he is damaged beyond recovery. A car crash kills Willem, Malcolm, and Malcolm's wife Sophie. Without Willem, Jude's health and will to live deteriorate despite the efforts of Harold and his remaining friends, and he eventually dies by suicide. Harold and JB are left to remember the family and friendships they lost.

recaps.text: Willem, JB, Malcolm, and Jude, friends since college, try to establish themselves in New York. Willem works in restaurants while auditioning as an actor; JB pursues art; Malcolm joins an architecture firm; and Jude enters the law. Their different backgrounds and ambitions create small rivalries, but the four remain closely attached. Jude is the most mysterious of them. He has no family history he is willing to share, walks with a limp, and experiences attacks of severe pain. Willem, who lives with him, quietly helps when Jude permits it. The friends understand that Jude's injuries and guardedness have roots in his childhood, but his refusal to discuss them establishes a boundary even his closest companions do not cross.

The friends' lives expand as their careers begin to take shape. Jude becomes a formidable litigator, Willem starts to receive better acting work, JB attracts attention as an artist, and Malcolm struggles to define himself apart from his wealthy family. Jude grows close to his former professor Harold Stein and Harold's wife, Julia. Their patient welcome gradually gives him an experience of family, and Harold eventually adopts him as an adult. Glimpses of Jude's earlier life explain why he finds this bond difficult to trust: after a childhood without parents and years in institutions, he expects affection to be conditional. His physician Andy knows that Jude injures himself and repeatedly tries to persuade him to accept more help, but Jude continues to conceal the extent of the danger from his friends.

Success changes the balance among the four friends. Willem becomes a prominent actor, Jude rises within his firm, and Malcolm receives major architectural work. JB builds a celebrated series of paintings from his friends' lives, but drug dependence makes him unreliable and cruel. During a confrontation he imitates Jude's impaired walk, turning the disability Jude is most ashamed of into a spectacle. The betrayal breaks JB's relationship with Jude and Willem. JB enters treatment and begins rebuilding his life, but forgiveness is slow and incomplete. The group no longer has the easy unity of its youth, even as the friends remain linked by history, professional achievement, and concern for Jude.

Jude begins a relationship with Caleb Porter, a fashion executive whose initial attentiveness gives way to contempt for Jude's disability and then physical abuse. Jude hides what is happening, convinced that he deserves it and afraid of losing even a harmful relationship. Caleb's violence escalates into a severe assault. Willem discovers enough of the aftermath to understand the danger and helps end Caleb's access to Jude, but Jude responds to the accumulated fear and shame by attempting suicide. His survival brings the people closest to him into direct contact with a crisis they had sensed but never fully seen. Harold, Julia, Willem, and Andy try to keep him safe, while Jude remains unable to believe that their love can outweigh his view of himself.

Willem's devotion to Jude develops into a romantic partnership. Physical intimacy is difficult for Jude, but Willem accepts boundaries and builds their shared life around companionship, travel, work, and care. Malcolm designs them a country house, and for several years Jude has a stability he once thought impossible: a loving partner, adoptive parents, close friends, and a distinguished legal career. He continues to live with pain and the effects of trauma, yet Willem gives him reasons to imagine a future. That period ends suddenly when a car crash kills Willem, Malcolm, and Malcolm's wife, Sophie. Jude loses both his partner and one of the friends who had known him since youth, while JB becomes the only other survivor of the original four.

After the crash, Jude continues working and remains connected to Harold, Julia, Andy, Richard, and JB, but grief removes the structure Willem had given his life. His physical condition worsens and his self-harm returns with greater severity. Memories disclose the childhood he has spent decades concealing: abuse at the monastery, Brother Luke's manipulation and exploitation, further violence after Luke's death, and the injury that left Jude with permanent damage. These experiences explain his reflexive shame without validating it, yet Jude cannot adopt the more compassionate understanding offered by the people who love him. Their vigilance prolongs his life but cannot restore his belief in a future. He ultimately dies by suicide, leaving Harold and the remaining friends to confront the limits of the care they offered.

Harold reflects on Jude's life and death from the position of a grieving father. He remembers the happiness of adopting Jude and the years in which their family seemed to prove that a damaged beginning did not have to determine an entire life. He also revisits the warnings, crises, and repeated attempts to keep Jude alive, knowing that love did not erase Jude's suffering. Julia shares his loss, and JB remains connected to them as the sole survivor of the four young men whose friendship opened the story. Harold cannot turn Jude's death into a consoling lesson. What remains is the record of a chosen family, the real happiness it created, and the enduring grief carried by those who outlive Jude, Willem, Malcolm, and Sophie.

characters.description: A clever, imaginative seven-year-old brought from India to Miss Minchin's London school while her widowed father returns abroad. Sara has been raised in comfort but dislikes being valued for money. She treats stories and make-believe as ways to understand people, and she is determined to behave with dignity and kindness.
characters.name: Sara Crewe

characters.description: Sara's affectionate father, a wealthy young army captain who has raised her alone since her mother's death. He and Sara are deeply attached, and leaving her at school causes both of them pain.
characters.name: Captain Crewe

characters.description: The head of the London school where Captain Crewe leaves Sara. Miss Minchin is outwardly attentive to her wealthy new pupil and enjoys the prestige Sara brings, but her warmth is formal and closely tied to status.
characters.name: Miss Minchin

characters.description: Miss Minchin's gentler sister and assistant at the school. She is easily flustered and usually yields to her sister's stronger will.
characters.name: Miss Amelia

characters.description: Sara's French maid, who accompanies her to school and is delighted to discover that Sara already speaks fluent French.
characters.name: Mariette

characters.description: An older pupil who resents Sara's special treatment and social position. Lavinia is proud of having been the school's leading student before Sara arrived and often tries to expose what she sees as Sara's pretensions.
characters.name: Lavinia Herbert

characters.description: A kind, insecure pupil who struggles badly with her lessons and is accustomed to being mocked for it. Sara befriends her and uses stories to make difficult schoolwork easier to grasp.
characters.name: Ermengarde St. John

characters.description: The youngest child at the school, a motherless four-year-old prone to loud tantrums. Sara calms her with sympathy rather than punishment, and Lottie begins to treat Sara as a substitute mother.
characters.name: Lottie Legh

characters.description: A hungry, exhausted scullery maid at Miss Minchin's school. Becky works from before dawn until late at night and sleeps in the attic, but Sara speaks to her as an equal and shares both food and stories with her.
characters.name: Becky

characters.description: The solicitor who arrives during Sara's birthday celebration with news about Captain Crewe's affairs. Brusque and concerned with unpaid bills, he informs Miss Minchin that the expected fortune has been lost.
characters.name: Mr. Barrow

characters.description: A rat living in the attic walls. Sara names him Melchisedec and gradually earns his trust with crumbs, making him part of the imaginary household that helps her endure isolation.
characters.name: Melchisedec

characters.description: An ailing Englishman recently returned from India who moves into the house adjoining the school. He is burdened by the disappearance of his late business partner's daughter and has asked friends to search for her.
characters.name: Tom Carrisford

characters.description: An Indian servant in Mr. Carrisford's household. From the neighboring roof he notices Sara in the attic and understands that her bare room and thin clothes conceal a lively imagination and severe hardship.
characters.name: Ram Dass

characters.description: Mr. Carrisford's solicitor and trusted friend, who has been traveling in search of Captain Crewe's missing daughter. His warm family life briefly intersects with Sara when one of his children sees her in the street.
characters.name: Mr. Carmichael

recaps.ending: Mr. Carrisford discovers that the poorly dressed girl from the neighboring attic is Sara Crewe, the daughter of his dead business partner. Captain Crewe's investment was not lost after all: the diamond mines succeeded, leaving Sara a large fortune that Carrisford has been managing while searching for her. Sara leaves Miss Minchin's school to live in his welcoming house, and Becky becomes her companion rather than a servant. Miss Minchin tries to recover control when she realizes what has happened, but Sara no longer depends on her and declines to return. Lavinia recognizes that Sara's conduct in poverty proved the quality she once claimed in comfort. Remembering the hunger she suffered, Sara arranges with a baker to feed any needy child who comes to the shop. There she learns that the beggar girl to whom she gave buns has been taken in and given work. Sara's wealth and security are restored, but her response is shaped by the hardship that taught her how unseen deprivation can be.
recaps.in_short: Sara Crewe, the imaginative daughter of a wealthy officer, is placed at Miss Minchin's London school and treated as its show pupil. She befriends neglected children and servants, insisting that courtesy should not depend on rank. When her father dies after an apparently disastrous investment, Miss Minchin strips Sara of her possessions and forces her to work and sleep in the attic. Sara endures hunger, cold, and humiliation by sharing stories with Becky and imagining that dignity is still possible. In the neighboring house, her father's former business partner, Tom Carrisford, is searching unsuccessfully for her while recovering the fortune he once believed lost. His servant Ram Dass secretly transforms Sara's attic with food, warmth, and furniture. A wandering monkey finally brings Sara into Carrisford's house, where her identity is recognized. Her fortune restored, Sara takes Becky with her and creates an arrangement to feed hungry children, using her recovery to relieve the suffering she now understands firsthand.

recaps.text: Seven-year-old Sara Crewe arrives in London from India with her widowed father, Captain Crewe, who enrolls her at Miss Minchin's school. Because Sara is rich, has costly clothes and a French maid, and is expected to inherit more wealth, Miss Minchin makes her the school's favored pupil. Sara is serious and imaginative rather than vain. She already speaks French, surprising the teacher, and her intelligence makes the older Lavinia jealous. Sara befriends Ermengarde, a pupil who struggles with lessons, and offers to help her through stories and patient explanations. Though separated from her adored father, Sara begins building friendships based on sympathy rather than the social rank that matters so much to Miss Minchin.

Sara comforts four-year-old Lottie, whose tantrums grow from grief for her dead mother, and allows the child to think of her as an adopted mother. She also notices Becky, the school's overworked scullery maid, asleep from exhaustion. Instead of reporting her, Sara offers food, conversation, and stories, treating Becky with a respect she rarely receives. Sara tells Ermengarde that she tries to imagine herself a princess so that she will remember to act generously even when nobody is watching. Meanwhile, Captain Crewe writes excitedly about investing with an old friend in newly discovered diamond mines. Miss Minchin is delighted by the prospect of even greater wealth and plans an elaborate birthday celebration for Sara, strengthening the school's display of her as its prized pupil.

During Sara's lavish eleventh-birthday party, the solicitor Mr. Barrow arrives with devastating news. Captain Crewe has died after illness and financial distress, and the diamond-mine venture appears to have consumed his entire fortune. With bills unpaid and no known relative to claim Sara, Miss Minchin immediately turns on the child she had flattered. She confiscates Sara's possessions, sends away her maid, and considers putting her into the street before deciding that an unpaid servant may be useful. Sara is moved into a bare attic room near Becky and made to teach younger pupils, run errands, and perform household work. Hungry and grieving, she is now scolded for the qualities that were praised when she was rich. Ermengarde and Lottie remain loyal, while Sara tries to preserve her self-command under Miss Minchin's cruelty.

Two years into her life as a servant, Sara is thin, poorly clothed, and frequently hungry, yet she continues sharing scraps and stories with Becky. She befriends an attic rat she names Melchisedec and imagines that the bleak room can still contain a household of its own. A sick man named Tom Carrisford moves into the neighboring house after returning from India. Unknown to Sara, he was Captain Crewe's partner in the diamond venture. The mines eventually proved successful, but Carrisford remains tormented by his role in his friend's despair and by his failure to find Crewe's daughter. His solicitor, Mr. Carmichael, continues searching abroad on the mistaken assumption that she was taken to school in France. Ram Dass, Carrisford's Indian servant, sees Sara through an attic window and becomes interested in the neglected child living next door.

On a freezing errand, Sara finds a coin and asks a baker whether she may spend it. Though desperately hungry, she gives most of the buns she buys to an even hungrier girl outside the shop. Back at the school, Ermengarde secretly brings food from a family parcel to the attic, creating a feast for Sara and Becky, but Miss Minchin discovers it and takes everything away. After this humiliation, Sara wakes to what seems like the fulfillment of her own imagining: a fire burns in the grate, the bed has warm coverings, the room holds food and useful furniture, and new gifts appear. Ram Dass and Carrisford's secretary have crossed the roof and furnished the attic after Carrisford, moved by the account of Sara's hardship, authorized them to help her anonymously. Sara and Becky call the unexplained transformation magic, unaware of the connection between their benefactor and Sara's father.

Carrisford's pet monkey escapes into Sara's attic during bad weather. Sara carries it next door and meets Carrisford, who is startled to learn that she was born in India and is Captain Crewe's daughter. Mr. Carmichael confirms that the missing child has been living beside them all along. The diamond mines succeeded, and Sara is the heir to the fortune Carrisford has safeguarded. She moves into his house, forgives him for the failed search, and asks that Becky live with her as a companion. Miss Minchin attempts to reclaim Sara once her wealth is known, but Sara calmly refuses to return to the school. Remembering her own hunger, she arranges to pay the local baker for food given to children in need. The first beneficiary is the girl who received Sara's buns; the baker has already taken her in and calls her Anne. Sara ends the story secure with Carrisford and Becky, using her restored fortune to help others survive the deprivation she experienced.

characters.description: A fifty-nine-year-old widower with rigid principles, practical skill, and little patience for rules he considers foolish. Recently forced out of his job, he patrols his housing development each morning, correcting parking violations and other lapses. His blunt manner conceals grief and a deeply rooted belief that actions matter more than talk.
characters.name: Ove

characters.description: Ove's late wife, whose absence governs his solitary routines. Warm, expressive, and interested in books and people, she could reach parts of Ove that he rarely showed anyone else. The house and neighborhood remain full of reminders of their life together.
characters.name: Sonja

characters.description: Ove's pregnant new neighbor, an Iranian immigrant who arrives with her husband and two daughters. Perceptive, determined, and unimpressed by Ove's attempts to keep everyone at a distance, she quickly discovers that his complaints are often followed by practical help.
characters.name: Parvaneh

characters.description: Parvaneh's good-natured Swedish husband, whose difficulty reversing a trailer into the development brings the new family into immediate conflict with Ove. He works in information technology and lacks Ove's confidence with tools and repairs.
characters.name: Patrick

characters.description: Parvaneh and Patrick's three-year-old daughter. Openly affectionate and direct, she is curious about the irritable man next door and soon treats him as part of the family's world.
characters.name: Nasanin

characters.description: A thin, battered stray that persists around Ove's house despite his disapproval. Independent and difficult to intimidate, the cat becomes another neighborhood responsibility that Ove claims not to want.
characters.name: The Cat

characters.description: Ove's neighbor and former close friend, now confined to a wheelchair after a stroke. The men once worked together to organize the housing development but fell out after years of rivalry, including fierce disagreement over their preferred makes of car.
characters.name: Rune

characters.description: Rune's wife and Sonja's old friend. She cares for Rune at home and has continued treating Ove as a neighbor despite the long breach between the two men. Her quiet persistence connects the present community to its earlier friendships.
characters.name: Anita

characters.description: An overweight young neighbor with an easygoing manner and a strong interest in food. He has lived near Ove long enough to understand that the older man's hostility is not the whole of his character.
characters.name: Jimmy

characters.description: A young man whom Ove first confronts over a bicycle he believes is being stolen. Adrian works at a cafe and has more mechanical curiosity than experience, making Ove's practical knowledge useful to him.
characters.name: Adrian

characters.description: Adrian's reserved friend, who works with him at a cafe. He is wary of Ove's temper but is drawn into the growing network of younger neighbors who rely on Ove's practical assistance.
characters.name: Mirsad

characters.description: A persistent local journalist who wants to interview Ove after a public rescue. He distrusts publicity and tries to evade her, while she recognizes that his reluctant heroism is a story worth pursuing.
characters.name: Lena

aliases: The man in the white shirt
characters.description: A municipal official involved in plans to move Rune out of his home and into institutional care. His impersonal confidence and reliance on administrative authority make him the focus of Ove's anger at systems that disregard individual lives.
characters.name: Social Services Official

recaps.ending: Ove's neighbors unite to prevent the authorities from removing Rune from Anita's care. Their testimony, records, and Lena's ability to expose the case defeat the official's plan. During the confrontation Ove collapses, and the hospital discovers that his heart is enlarged and may fail without warning. He responds by returning to the community that has formed around him. Parvaneh gives birth to a son, and Ove becomes an honorary grandfather to her children. He teaches, repairs, watches over the neighborhood, and remains close to the cat and the friends who have claimed him. Several years later, after he fails to clear the snow outside his house, Parvaneh finds that he has died peacefully in bed with the cat beside him. Ove has left practical instructions for his funeral and provisions for those he loves. Far more people attend than the solitary ceremony he expected, demonstrating the extent of the community he built while insisting that he needed no one.
recaps.in_short: Widowed, forcibly retired, and determined to join his late wife Sonja, Ove repeatedly tries to end his life. Each attempt is interrupted by a neighbor who needs him. Pregnant Parvaneh and her family draw him into driving lessons, childcare, repairs, and friendship; a stray cat moves into his house; and younger neighbors seek his protection and practical knowledge. Memories reveal a life shaped by honest work, Sonja's love, bereavement, and repeated battles with indifferent institutions. In the present, Ove rallies the neighborhood to stop officials from taking his disabled former friend Rune away from Anita. The effort succeeds, but Ove's collapse reveals a dangerous heart condition. He abandons his suicide plans and becomes a grandfather figure within the improvised family around him. Years later he dies peacefully at home. His crowded funeral and the people he has provided for show that the isolated man became the center of a lasting community.

recaps.text: Ove is a fifty-nine-year-old widower whose days are governed by rules, inspections of his housing development, and irritation with other people. He has recently been pushed into retirement and sees little reason to continue without his wife, Sonja. His plan for an orderly death is disrupted when new neighbors arrive and Patrick backs a trailer into Ove's mailbox. Patrick's pregnant wife, Parvaneh, is direct enough to challenge Ove and practical enough to keep asking for help. Their daughters respond to him without fear. Ove complains about the family's incompetence but fixes the damage and becomes entangled in their affairs. At the same time, a battered stray cat repeatedly appears near his house. Flashbacks begin to show the disciplined childhood and devotion to honest work beneath Ove's abrasive routines.

Ove attempts to hang himself so he can be reunited with Sonja, but the attempt fails and the neighbors' needs again intrude. Patrick is injured in an accident, and Parvaneh depends on Ove for transport and help with the children. Although he insists on strict boundaries, he repeatedly does what the situation requires. He takes responsibility for the half-frozen stray cat rather than let it die. He also confronts two young men over a bicycle, only to learn that Adrian is repairing it rather than stealing it. The present-day encounters are interwoven with Ove's early life: his father taught him to work, repair things, and remain honest; after his father's death, Ove endured loss and unfairness without surrendering those principles. His stubborn competence, which isolates him socially, is also what makes others seek him out.

Ove makes further attempts to die, but each turns into another obligation to the living. At a railway platform he abandons his plan and saves a man who falls onto the tracks. The rescue attracts journalist Lena, whose requests for an interview he tries to avoid. Parvaneh insists that Ove teach her to drive, forcing him into regular contact with her and giving him a task that suits his belief in doing things properly. The cat settles into his home, and Adrian and his friend Mirsad enter his circle. Memories show Ove meeting Sonja on a train and being transformed by her delight in books, color, and conversation. She recognizes his reliability without trying to make him socially polished. Their courtship explains why the quiet house and empty routines of the present feel unbearable to him.

Ove's driving lessons with Parvaneh deepen their trust, and she refuses to let his harsh self-judgments define him. His circle widens as he repairs bicycles, helps Adrian, and gives Mirsad refuge after the young man is rejected by his family for being gay. Ove's history with Sonja also becomes clearer. A bus crash during a trip left her permanently injured and ended their hope of having a child. Faced with inaccessible buildings and indifferent officials, Ove renovated their home and fought for her right to work as a teacher. Sonja continued creating relationships and purpose despite what they lost. Her later death from cancer left Ove alone with the battles and routines they had shared. In the present, Anita tells Ove that officials intend to remove her disabled husband Rune from their home, reviving Ove's anger at bureaucratic decisions imposed on vulnerable people.

Ove decides that Rune will not be taken away if the neighborhood can prevent it. This commitment reverses his withdrawal: instead of arranging his own death, he organizes other people around a concrete fight. Parvaneh, Patrick, Jimmy, Adrian, Mirsad, Anita, and Lena each contribute knowledge, evidence, practical help, or public pressure. Ove also reconciles himself to defending Rune despite the rivalry that ended their friendship years earlier. The people he has helped now help him, turning a collection of interruptions into a community. Lena's reporting and the neighbors' preparation weaken the social services official's power to treat Rune as an isolated case. Ove remains outwardly irritable and exacting, but his actions openly affirm that he considers these neighbors his responsibility and that he is again invested in what happens next.

The campaign succeeds, and Rune remains at home with Anita. During the final confrontation Ove collapses and is hospitalized. Doctors explain that his unusually enlarged heart could fail, news that the neighborhood receives with both fear and an appreciation of its accidental symbolism. Ove returns home rather than resuming his suicide plans. Parvaneh gives birth to a boy, and Ove becomes an honorary grandfather to all three children. Over the following years he continues teaching, repairing, enforcing rules, and caring for the people around him. One winter morning Parvaneh notices that his path has not been cleared and finds him dead peacefully in bed, with the cat beside him. He has left instructions and made financial provision for the people he regards as family. His funeral draws hundreds, far exceeding the small gathering he requested. Ove's life ends not in the isolation he had planned but at the center of the community his reluctant acts of service created.

characters.description: The newly appointed ambassador from Lsel Station, a small independent mining habitat, sent to represent her home at the dazzling and dangerous heart of the vast Teixcalaanli Empire. A lifelong lover of Teixcalaanli poetry and culture, she is nonetheless an outsider determined to protect Lsel's independence. She arrives to find her predecessor dead and quickly realizes she has walked into a web of politics and murder she barely understands, with little support and less time.
characters.name: Mahit Dzmare

characters.description: A quick, elegant young Teixcalaanli official assigned as Mahit's cultural liaison, or asekreta, tasked with guiding the new ambassador through the customs, language, and etiquette of the City. Clever, ambitious, and genuinely curious, she becomes Mahit's closest ally and interpreter, helping her navigate a court where every phrase and gesture carries hidden meaning.
characters.name: Three Seagrass

characters.description: Mahit's predecessor as Lsel's ambassador to Teixcalaan, who served for many years and is found dead as the story begins. Charismatic and deeply enmeshed in imperial affairs, he left behind unfinished dealings and dangerous secrets. Lsel technology preserves a recorded imprint of his memories and personality, meant to guide his successor, making him a presence in Mahit's mind as well as a mystery she must solve.
characters.name: Yskandr Aghavn

characters.description: A powerful and self-possessed member of the Emperor's inner circle, close enough to the throne to shape events. Sharp, watchful, and hard to read, she takes an interest in Mahit's survival and offers a measure of protection, though her own aims in the unfolding crisis remain guarded. She is among the most formidable figures Mahit must learn to deal with.
characters.name: Nineteen Adze

characters.description: The aging Emperor of Teixcalaan, who has ruled long and now faces the pressing question of who will succeed him. Shrewd and weary, he had his own private dealings with Mahit's predecessor, and the shape of the succession he leaves behind hangs over the entire capital as ambitious figures maneuver for the throne.
characters.name: Six Direction

characters.description: A friend and fellow official of Three Seagrass, charming and a bit reckless, who is drawn into helping Mahit investigate the dangers surrounding her. His willingness to bend rules makes him useful and his connections handy as the intrigue deepens.
characters.name: Twelve Azalea

characters.description: A popular and ambitious military commander whose growing support among the soldiery and the crowds makes him a serious contender for imperial power. His rise threatens to tip the succession crisis into open conflict, putting him at odds with those trying to keep the transition orderly and the City at peace.
characters.name: One Lightning

recaps.ending: The succession crisis breaks into violence in the capital, but it is resolved not by the ambitious general One Lightning seizing the throne but by the old Emperor Six Direction giving up his own life in a public act designed to trigger an orderly succession and deny the coup its opening. In the aftermath, his trusted ally Nineteen Adze takes the throne as the new ruler of Teixcalaan. Mahit, having pieced together that her predecessor Yskandr had tried to trade Lsel's memory-implant technology for imperial protection, and that her own implant was sabotaged by a faction back home to stop exactly that, manages to preserve Lsel's independence. She refuses to surrender the station's secret technology to the Empire and keeps the most dangerous truths hidden. Loving Teixcalaanli culture yet fearing being consumed by it, she decides she cannot stay, and parts from Three Seagrass, whose bond with her has deepened, with the door left open between them. She turns toward home carrying the knowledge that something unknown and threatening is moving at the edge of Lsel's space, a danger that will shape what comes next.
recaps.in_short: Mahit Dzmare arrives at the capital of the Teixcalaanli Empire as the new ambassador from tiny, independent Lsel Station, only to find her predecessor Yskandr dead and her implanted memory-copy of him, meant to guide her, failing. Aided by her sharp liaison Three Seagrass, she investigates his death and uncovers that Yskandr had secretly bargained with the aging Emperor Six Direction, offering Lsel's prized memory-implant technology in exchange for the Empire's protection. As a succession crisis erupts and the ambitious general One Lightning moves toward a coup, Mahit realizes her own implant was deliberately sabotaged from home by a Lsel faction opposed to that bargain, and that Lsel's independence and its secret technology are the true stakes. To halt the coup and force an orderly succession, Emperor Six Direction sacrifices his own life, and his ally Nineteen Adze rises to the throne. Mahit secures Lsel's continued independence, refuses to hand over its technology, and, unwilling to be swallowed by the culture she loves, chooses to return home, while an unknown threat stirs at the edge of Lsel's space.

recaps.text: Mahit Dzmare travels from Lsel Station, a small independent habitat, to serve as its ambassador at the center of the immense Teixcalaanli Empire, a civilization whose language, poetry, and rituals she has admired all her life. On arrival she learns that her predecessor, Yskandr, is dead, apparently for some time, and that no one will give her a straight account of how he died. She is assigned a poised imperial liaison, Three Seagrass, to guide her through the City's customs. Complicating everything, the Lsel memory-implant that should carry Yskandr's experience and advice inside her head is not working as it should, leaving her almost alone in a place where a misjudged word can be fatal. She begins to suspect Yskandr was murdered and that she may be a target too.

Settling uneasily into the ambassador's residence, Mahit works with Three Seagrass to investigate Yskandr's death and finds that he was far more entangled in imperial politics than Lsel ever knew. The Empire is on edge over the looming question of who will succeed its aging Emperor, and factions are already maneuvering. Mahit gains a wary, powerful potential ally in the influential Nineteen Adze, but an attempt on her life makes plain how exposed she is. She realizes that the answers about Yskandr are bound up with dangerous secrets at the highest levels of the City, and that simply surviving will require her to understand a political game whose rules she is still learning.

Mahit uncovers that Yskandr had been conducting his own private negotiations with the Emperor Six Direction, dangling something Lsel guards very closely in exchange for the Empire's protection of the station. As she pieces this together, the succession crisis intensifies: the ambitious and popular military commander One Lightning gathers support that could carry him to the throne by force, and rival figures at court press their own claims. Unrest spreads through the City itself. Caught between loyalty to Lsel and her fascination with Teixcalaan, Mahit must decide whom she can trust while the stakes rise from her personal safety to the fate of nations.

The crisis tips toward open conflict as One Lightning's bid for power drives the City toward civil war, with violence reaching its streets. Mahit comes to understand that her malfunctioning memory-implant was not an accident but was deliberately sabotaged by a faction back on Lsel, one determined to stop Yskandr's bargain and keep the station's technology out of imperial hands. She grasps that Lsel's independence, and the secret of the very technology inside her own head, are the true prize being fought over. Working with Three Seagrass and her allies, she tries to steer events so that Lsel is not swallowed by the Empire nor destroyed in the chaos, even as the throne itself hangs in the balance.

To break the coup and force an orderly transfer of power, the old Emperor Six Direction takes his own life in a deliberate public act, denying One Lightning his path to the throne. In the settling of affairs, the formidable Nineteen Adze becomes the new ruler of Teixcalaan. Mahit, having exposed the tangled scheme around Yskandr's death and her sabotaged implant, secures Lsel's continued independence and refuses to hand over the station's memory-implant technology, keeping its most dangerous secrets safe. Though she loves Teixcalaanli culture and has grown close to Three Seagrass, she decides she cannot remain without losing herself to the Empire, and she chooses to return home. She leaves carrying the unsettling knowledge that an unknown threat is stirring at the far edge of Lsel's space, a shadow over whatever comes next.

characters.description: The Dragon Reborn, the champion who must confront the Dark One at the Last Battle. Calm, resolute, and quietly awesome in his power over the cleansed male One Power, missing his left hand, he has united many of the nations and now stands ready to lead the world into Tarmon Gai'don and to face the Shadow at Shayol Ghul itself.
characters.name: Rand al'Thor

characters.description: A ta'veren gambler and brilliant, reluctant battle commander from the Two Rivers, one-eyed after the price he paid rescuing Moiraine, carrying the memories of dead generals and a medallion that turns aside the One Power. Husband to the Seanchan Empress and holder of the Horn of Valere's fate, he is one of the few who can turn the tide of a battlefield by instinct.
characters.name: Mat Cauthon

characters.description: A blacksmith, wolfbrother, and battle lord from the Two Rivers, master of the world of dreams and able to speak with wolves. At peace at last with his gifts and his wife, Faile, at his side, he commands a great army and stands ready to guard the Dragon Reborn wherever the fight leads.
characters.name: Perrin Aybara

characters.description: The Amyrlin Seat of a reunited White Tower, young but formidable, having broken a usurper and the Black Ajah's grip on the sisters. She leads the Aes Sedai into the Last Battle and presses the nations to bind themselves to a lasting peace, wary of the Dragon Reborn's plan to break the seals on the Dark One's prison.
characters.name: Egwene al'Vere

characters.description: The Queen of Andor and Cairhien, an Aes Sedai, one of the women bound to Rand and carrying his children. Proud, capable, and determined to lead from the front, she takes a central role in commanding the united armies of the Light.
characters.name: Elayne Trakand

characters.description: The former Wisdom of Emond's Field, an Aes Sedai and the most gifted Healer of her age, wife to Lan. Fierce and stubborn, she is one of Rand's closest companions and means to stand beside him to the very end, whatever it demands of her.
characters.name: Nynaeve al'Meara

characters.description: The uncrowned king of Malkier and one of the deadliest swordsmen alive, bonded to his wife, Nynaeve. Having raised an army on his ride north, he holds the line at Tarwin's Gap against the Shadow's hordes pouring out of the Blight.
characters.name: Lan Mandragoran

characters.description: The Aes Sedai who first found the Dragon Reborn and set his path, believed dead for years until Mat rescued her from beyond the twisted Tower of Ghenjei. Weakened but wise and unbending, she returns to guide Rand and to help hold the fractious rulers to a common cause at the last.
characters.name: Moiraine Damodred

characters.description: A practical young woman who reads glimpses of the future in the auras she alone can see, and a keen scholar of prophecy. One of the three women who love Rand, she works to interpret the omens that may decide the Last Battle.
characters.name: Min Farshaw

characters.description: A full Wise One of the Aiel, once a warrior, proud and fiercely honest, a strong channeler. One of the three women tied to Rand by love and prophecy, she takes her place among the Aiel forces committed to the Last Battle.
characters.name: Aviendha

characters.description: Now Fortuona, Empress of the Seanchan, small, composed, and ruthless, wed by her people's custom to Mat Cauthon. Ruler of a vast empire whose armies collar channelers as weapons, she weighs whether and how to bring her power to bear against the Shadow.
characters.name: Tuon

characters.description: A legendary and formidable Aes Sedai, imperious and shrewd, long a difficult mentor to the Dragon Reborn. Respected and feared in equal measure, she remains close to the center of events as the Light marshals for the end.
characters.name: Cadsuane Melaidhrin

recaps.ending: A Memory of Light ends with the Shadow defeated and the world remade at terrible cost. The forces of the Light win Tarmon Gai'don, but many fall: Egwene al'Vere dies unleashing a power that turns the enemy's channelers against themselves; Gawyn Trakand, Siuan Sanche, and the great captain Gareth Bryne are among the dead; Lan Mandragoran slays the Forsaken Demandred in a duel and barely survives. The twisted peddler Padan Fain is killed by Mat. Perrin destroys the assassin Slayer and guards Rand in the world of dreams. At Shayol Ghul, Rand confronts the Dark One directly and chooses not to annihilate him, for a world stripped of the ability to choose evil would be a world of puppets; instead he seals the prison anew and closes the Bore. Bound soul to soul with his enemy Moridin, Rand walks out of the fighting in Moridin's healthy body while his own broken body is burned on a pyre. The world believes the Dragon dead, but he lives, anonymous and finally free, riding away alone. Min, Aviendha, and Elayne, who carries his children, keep his secret. The Wheel of Time turns onward into a new Age.
recaps.in_short: Tarmon Gai'don, the Last Battle, is fought at last. At the Field of Merrilor the nations bind themselves to the Dragon's Peace, and Rand goes to Shayol Ghul to face the Dark One while four great battlefronts hold the Shadow's armies of Trollocs, Sharans, and Forsaken. Lan holds Tarwin's Gap and, in single combat, kills the Forsaken general Demandred. Egwene falls destroying an army of Shadow channelers; Gawyn, Siuan, and the great captain Gareth Bryne are among the many dead. Mat, become the Light's supreme commander, turns the tide and the Horn of Valere is sounded to call the heroes of legend. In the Pit of Doom, aided by Nynaeve and Moiraine, Rand battles the Dark One in a contest of wills and visions, refusing to destroy him utterly because that would end humanity's freedom to choose, and instead reseals his prison. Rand's dying body is burned on a pyre, but his soul lives on in another man's body, and he slips away unknown, free at last, while Min, Aviendha, and Elayne, who carries his children, keep the secret. The Wheel turns, and a new Age begins.

recaps.text: Rand al'Thor of the Two Rivers was revealed as the Dragon Reborn, prophesied to fight the Dark One at the Last Battle and to break the world again. Guided out of hiding by the Aes Sedai Moiraine with his ta'veren friends Mat and Perrin, he claimed the sword Callandor, was accepted by the Aiel, conquered nations, killed several of the Forsaken, founded the Black Tower, and did the impossible by cleansing the male One Power of its taint, though he lost his left hand along the way. His friends rose with him: Perrin became a wolfbrother and battle lord and freed his wife, Faile; Mat, a peerless battle commander wed to the Seanchan heir Tuon, lost an eye rescuing the long-lost Moiraine from beyond the Tower of Ghenjei; Egwene broke a usurper to become Amyrlin of a reunited White Tower and shattered the Black Ajah's grip; Elayne won the thrones of Andor and Cairhien. After nearly falling to despair and madness, Rand was remade into a calm, certain man ready for the end. Now the seals on the Dark One's prison are breaking, Rand has declared he will shatter them and face the Dark One directly, and he has called the rulers of the world to the Field of Merrilor. Lan rides to hold Tarwin's Gap, and the nations gather for Tarmon Gai'don, the Last Battle.

characters.description: The capable mistress of Little Paddocks. She supports an assorted household of relatives, friends, and lodgers, and responds calmly when a newspaper notice predicts a murder in her home.
characters.name: Letitia Blacklock

characters.description: Letitia Blacklock's affectionate, muddle-headed childhood friend. She lives at Little Paddocks and depends heavily on Letitia, whom she has known for many years.
characters.name: Dora Bunner

characters.description: A young man staying at Little Paddocks as one of Miss Blacklock's distant relations. Cheerful and theatrical, he treats the announced murder as entertainment until the shooting makes it real.
characters.name: Patrick Simmons

characters.description: A reserved young woman presented as Patrick's sister and another distant relation of Miss Blacklock. She is less open than Patrick about her reasons for being in Chipping Cleghorn.
characters.name: Julia Simmons

characters.description: A widowed mother lodging at Little Paddocks and working in a nearby garden. Quiet and self-contained, she is supporting her young son while his father is presumed lost in the war.
characters.name: Phillipa Haymes

characters.description: The volatile Central European cook at Little Paddocks. Traumatized by wartime persecution, she expects suspicion to fall on her and expresses every fear with dramatic intensity.
characters.name: Mitzi

characters.description: A young Swiss employee of a local hotel. He appears at Little Paddocks during the gathering prompted by the newspaper notice and enters the darkened room carrying a weapon.
characters.name: Rudi Scherz

characters.description: The county police officer leading the investigation. Methodical but imaginative, he takes Miss Marple's observations seriously as the case reaches into old identities and inheritances.
characters.name: Inspector Dermot Craddock

characters.description: An elderly visitor with a precise memory for social detail and a wide knowledge of ordinary dishonesty. She becomes involved through her acquaintance with the local vicar's wife.
characters.name: Miss Jane Marple

characters.description: A forthright farmer who lives nearby with Amy Murgatroyd. Her practical manner and close attention to the case make her an active participant rather than a passive village witness.
characters.name: Miss Hinchcliffe

characters.description: Miss Hinchcliffe's gentle companion. She was present during the shooting at Little Paddocks and later struggles to recover a crucial visual memory from the darkened room.
characters.name: Amy Murgatroyd

characters.description: A confident retired officer living in Chipping Cleghorn. He and his much younger wife attend the gathering at Little Paddocks after seeing the newspaper announcement.
characters.name: Colonel Easterbrook

characters.description: A local widow with a keen interest in village affairs. She and her son Edmund are among the neighbours who arrive at Little Paddocks expecting a party game.
characters.name: Mrs Swettenham

recaps.ending: Miss Marple and Inspector Craddock expose the woman called Letitia Blacklock as Charlotte Blacklock, Letitia's sister. The real Letitia died abroad, and Charlotte assumed her identity so that she could inherit when the elderly Belle Goedler died. Rudi Scherz recognized Charlotte from a Swiss clinic and became part of a staged robbery that she converted into his murder. Bunny's old memories and habit of calling her Lotty threatened the disguise, so Charlotte poisoned her; Amy Murgatroyd was killed after recalling that Miss Blacklock had not been in the room during the shooting. A trap using Mitzi and Miss Marple provokes Charlotte into attacking again, and she is arrested. Phillipa Haymes and Julia Simmons are revealed as the heirs Pip and Emma, and they inherit after Charlotte's scheme collapses.
recaps.in_short: A newspaper notice announces that a murder will occur at Letitia Blacklock's house. Curious neighbours gather; the lights fail, an armed man appears, and the intruder Rudi Scherz is shot dead. Further deaths show that the event concealed an old identity secret tied to an inheritance. Miss Marple discovers that the household's supposed Letitia is actually her sister Charlotte. The real Letitia died abroad, and Charlotte took her place to receive money due after Belle Goedler's death. Rudi recognized her, Bunny remembered too much, and Amy Murgatroyd recalled that she was absent during the staged shooting, so Charlotte killed all three. Miss Marple and Inspector Craddock trap her during another attempted attack. Charlotte is arrested, while Phillipa and Julia are identified as Pip and Emma, the alternative heirs.

recaps.text: The Chipping Cleghorn newspaper carries a notice stating that a murder will occur at Little Paddocks at 6:30 that evening. Letitia Blacklock denies placing it, but her neighbours arrive out of curiosity. Her household includes her old friend Bunny, the young relations Patrick and Julia Simmons, the lodger Phillipa Haymes, and the anxious cook Mitzi. At the appointed time the lights go out, a man shines a torch and orders everyone to raise their hands, and shots are fired. When the lights return, the intruder, hotel employee Rudi Scherz, is dead and Miss Blacklock has a wound to her ear. What looked like a prank or staged robbery has become a murder inquiry.

Inspector Craddock finds no simple explanation for the shooting. Rudi had a record of petty dishonesty and some contact with Miss Blacklock, but the room's layout, a recently oiled door, and the failure of the lights suggest advance preparation inside the house. Miss Marple joins the inquiry and studies the household's relationships. A large inheritance expected by Miss Blacklock depends on the death of the elderly Belle Goedler, while alternative heirs known only as Pip and Emma may be nearby under other names. Bunny's confused recollections of earlier years repeatedly unsettle Miss Blacklock, and small household incidents suggest that someone is increasingly afraid of what the old woman may remember.

Bunny dies after eating a poisoned birthday cake and taking medication from the wrong bedside table. Her death directs attention toward her habit of mixing past and present names. Meanwhile, Amy Murgatroyd works with Miss Hinchcliffe to reconstruct what she saw when the torch swept across the room. She realizes that one familiar person was not where everyone assumed during the blackout, but she is killed before she can report the name. Craddock investigates Miss Blacklock's life abroad and the history of her invalid sister Charlotte. Miss Marple concludes that the original shooting, the inheritance, and the household murders all depend on someone maintaining a false identity.

Miss Marple and Craddock reveal that the woman known as Letitia Blacklock is actually her sister Charlotte. Letitia died abroad, after which Charlotte assumed her identity to inherit Belle Goedler's fortune. Rudi Scherz had recognized Charlotte from a Swiss clinic; she arranged the supposed hold-up and shot him while using the darkness and a hidden route to preserve her role as victim. She later poisoned Bunny, whose memories exposed the name Lotty, and killed Amy Murgatroyd after Amy remembered her absence from the room. A staged confrontation involving Mitzi draws Charlotte into another attack, and she is caught trying to silence Miss Marple. Phillipa Haymes and Julia Simmons prove to be Pip and Emma, the alternative heirs, and Charlotte is arrested.

characters.description: A small, plump, unmemorable man, once an intelligence officer and now living quietly in Chelsea, no longer in government service. Scholarly, courteous and endlessly patient, he is a listener rather than an interrogator, and his talent is for noticing the detail that everyone else has smoothed over. He agrees to look into a reader's letter as a favour to a wartime colleague, and finds himself in a closed and self-satisfied world he understands well enough to see through.
characters.name: George Smiley

characters.description: The editor of a small nonconformist weekly with a devoted and elderly readership. Sensible, kind and conscientious, she worked in intelligence during the war, which is how she knows Smiley. A letter from a long-standing subscriber alarms her enough that she cannot simply file it, and she takes it to Smiley for advice.
characters.name: Ailsa Brimley

characters.description: The wife of a junior master at Carne, an ancient and expensive public school, and a faithful reader of the weekly to which she writes. Chapel-going, plainly dressed and known locally for her charity and good works, she is regarded by the school's wives as socially beneath them and by others as a modest, decent woman. Her letter states that her husband intends to kill her, and asks that nothing be done about it yet.
characters.name: Stella Rode

characters.description: A science master at Carne, the son of a small tradesman and a grammar-school and provincial university product, who has worked hard to acquire the manners of the place and is quietly despised for it. Anxious, punctilious and eager to belong, he is conscious at every moment of being an outsider among colleagues who were educated at schools like this one.
characters.name: Stanley Rode

characters.description: A detective inspector of the local county police handling the Carne case: solid, honest and shrewd, and well aware that investigating a great school means being managed by it at every turn. He knew Smiley's name from the war, welcomes his help, and shares his files with him more openly than his superiors would like.
characters.name: Rigby

characters.description: A senior housemaster at Carne, a large, theatrical and cultivated man in his last year before retirement, given to good wine, music and grand gestures, and to talking with practised indiscretion about the school he has served all his life. His brother served with Smiley during the war, which is the introduction that opens Carne's doors. Beneath the performance he is a disappointed man whose career never rose as far as he expected.
characters.name: Terence Fielding

characters.description: A master and the school's unofficial authority on precedence, dress and correct behaviour, fastidious to the point of absurdity and deeply invested in Carne's social hierarchy. He entertains carefully chosen guests, keeps house with his sister, and disapproves of the Rodes on grounds he would describe as taste.
characters.name: Felix D'Arcy

characters.description: D'Arcy's unmarried sister, who keeps house for him, breeds dogs and shares his views on who is and is not acceptable at Carne, expressed with rather less circumlocution than her brother uses.
characters.name: Dorothy D'Arcy

characters.description: The wife of one of the senior masters, a large, gracious woman who has spent decades in the school's society and reads it perfectly. Her conversation is elaborately polite and quietly destructive, and she dispenses gossip about her neighbours as a form of power. She is one of the few people at Carne who says anything about Stella Rode that is not simply admiring.
characters.name: Shane Hecht

characters.description: A vagrant woman, known locally as Mad Janie, who lives rough near the Rodes' house at the edge of the town and is treated by the town as a harmless lunatic. Stella Rode was kind to her, and she is found afterwards with belongings that were not hers. Her ramblings about what she saw that night are dismissed by almost everyone.
characters.name: Jane Lyn

characters.description: A boy in Fielding's house, amiable and not academically able, who is anxious about the examination results that will decide whether he can stay on at the school. He is grateful to his housemaster and reluctant to say anything that might reflect on him.
characters.name: Perkins

recaps.ending: Smiley establishes that Fielding had let the boy Perkins see an examination paper in advance so that he would not be removed from the school, and that Stella Rode obtained proof of it, along with knowledge of an earlier disgrace which Fielding had spent his career living down. Instead of exposing him she kept the evidence and let him understand that she had it, which was the private cruelty she practised on many people while the town admired her charity. With retirement and his reputation in front of him, Fielding killed her, and dressed the crime to point at her husband, whom Carne would have been happy to believe capable of it. When Perkins begins to talk about the examination paper, Fielding kills him too, in what is arranged to look like a road accident. Confronted with the reconstruction, Fielding admits what he did, and is arrested. Jane Lyn, who was the town's preferred culprit, is cleared. Stanley Rode is left innocent of the murder but with the truth about his marriage and no place at the school he tried so hard to enter. Smiley goes back to London with Ailsa Brimley, having exposed a killing that the school would rather have blamed on an outsider.
recaps.in_short: Ailsa Brimley, editor of a small nonconformist weekly, receives a letter from a reader, Stella Rode, saying that her husband intends to kill her, and takes it to her old wartime colleague George Smiley. Before anything can be done, Stella is beaten to death at her house on the edge of Carne, an ancient public school where her husband teaches science. Smiley goes down, is admitted to the school through the housemaster Terence Fielding, and works alongside Inspector Rigby. Carne assumes the murderer is either Stanley Rode, an outsider by birth and manner, or a local vagrant woman found with the dead woman's belongings; physical evidence has been arranged to incriminate the husband. Smiley finds that Stella's reputation for saintliness concealed a talent for collecting and using other people's shameful secrets. She had proof that Fielding had shown an examination paper to a boy in his house, and knowledge of an older disgrace that would have destroyed him. Fielding killed her to end it, staged the scene against Rode, and later killed the boy when he began to talk. Confronted, he confesses, and Smiley returns to London.

recaps.text: Ailsa Brimley edits a small nonconformist weekly with a loyal, mostly elderly readership. A letter arrives from Stella Rode, a long-standing subscriber and the daughter of a man the paper once honoured, saying plainly that her husband is planning to kill her, and asking that nothing be done for the moment. Uneasy, Ailsa takes it to George Smiley, with whom she worked in intelligence during the war and who is now retired and living quietly in London. Before they can decide how to respond, news comes that Stella Rode has been found beaten to death at North Fields, the house she shared with her husband on the edge of Carne, an ancient and expensive public school where he teaches science. The murder took place on a snowy night after a dinner at the house of Terence Fielding, a senior housemaster. Smiley travels down to Carne, where the county police, in the person of Inspector Rigby, are conducting an investigation hemmed in on all sides by the school's dislike of publicity.

Smiley is admitted to Carne society because Fielding's brother served with him in the war, and he begins to move between the school and the police station. Rigby shows him the case as it stands. Clothing belonging to Stanley Rode, along with other items, has been found in an outbuilding, footprints cross the snow, and the pattern of evidence points steadily at the husband. Rode himself is a nervous, meticulous man from a modest background who has laboured to be accepted at a school that will never accept him, and Carne's masters and their wives, among them the fastidious Felix D'Arcy and the formidably gracious Shane Hecht, make it clear that they regard him as a social intruder and would find his guilt unsurprising. The town, meanwhile, prefers a different culprit: Jane Lyn, a vagrant woman who lives near the house and has been found with belongings that had been Stella's. Smiley is struck by how conveniently the evidence has arranged itself and by how much everyone wishes to believe it.

Smiley begins to take apart the picture of the dead woman. Carne remembers Stella Rode as humble and charitable, active in her chapel, generous to the poor and to Jane Lyn in particular. What Smiley uncovers is a woman who studied the people around her for weaknesses and enjoyed possessing them: who humiliated her husband socially while appearing to support him, who told damaging stories in the guise of confidences, and who kept what she learned rather than using it openly. The letter she sent to the newspaper begins to look less like a frightened appeal than another move in a private campaign. At the same time Smiley picks at the physical evidence: the way the incriminating objects were placed, the timing of the walk home from Fielding's dinner and the movements of everyone who was at that table. The case against Rode is too complete, and the objects that convict him were left where they were certain to be found.

Attention narrows to Fielding, whose career at Carne is ending in disappointment and who is due to retire. Smiley learns that a boy in his house, Perkins, was in danger of being removed from the school after failing an examination, and that his paper was not what it should have been. Perkins is questioned and is frightened and evasive, unwilling to say anything against the housemaster who protected him. Shortly afterwards the boy is killed in what appears to be a road accident. Smiley concludes that Stella Rode had come by proof of what Fielding had done for the boy, and by knowledge of an older episode in his past that he had spent a lifetime burying, and that she had kept both without ever making a demand, so that he lived under her observation. The murder was Fielding's release from her, and the evidence in the outbuilding was placed to hang it on a husband nobody at Carne would defend.

Smiley sets his reconstruction in front of Fielding, who admits to killing Stella Rode and to killing Perkins when the boy began to talk, and he is arrested. Jane Lyn, whom the town had already convicted, is cleared. Stanley Rode is innocent of the murder, but the investigation has stripped away the marriage he defended: the wife everyone praised for her goodness had made a study of his shame, and he has no future at the school he tried to be worthy of. The masters and their wives close ranks around the school's reputation, less troubled by two deaths than by the noise. Smiley, who has no official standing and wanted none, leaves Carne with Ailsa Brimley and returns to London, having proved only that a closed community will believe any story that protects its own and blames an outsider.
